name: Insulin (bodybuilding use)

lead: Some bodybuilders use insulin hoping for fuller, bigger muscles. It is the body's main anabolic hormone and a prescription medicine for diabetes, and its use in bodybuilding is off-label.

Insulin promotes glucose uptake in muscle and fat, glycogen storage, amino-acid uptake and protein synthesis, and slows protein and fat breakdown. Users reportedly pair it with steroids and growth hormone. A reference article states the effects are supported only in a small group of drug-naive individuals, and whether insulin improves performance is unclear.

paras: Reported use is around training and meals, usually by experienced bodybuilders stacking it with other compounds, with carbohydrate intake alongside. It is a prescription drug and there is no medical protocol for this use.

The main risk is hypoglycemia, which can progress to seizures, coma, brain damage or death, and insulin misuse has been mentioned as a possible factor in bodybuilder deaths. It is prescription-only in many countries and banned for non-diabetic athletes.

angle.text: Some bodybuilders use prescription insulin believing it pushes glucose and amino acids into muscle for fuller muscle bellies and a more muscular physique. This is off-label use of a diabetes drug, and the effect has been shown only in a small group of drug-naive individuals.

lead: Insulin is a peptide hormone made by the pancreas that regulates blood glucose and is often described as the body's main anabolic hormone: it moves glucose into muscle and fat cells, increases amino-acid uptake and protein synthesis, and slows the liver's glucose output and the breakdown of fat and protein.[1] As a medicine it treats diabetes.[2]

In bodybuilding, insulin is used for a physique goal: fuller, rounder muscles and more efficient nutrient partitioning, meaning more of the calories eaten going to muscle glycogen and protein rather than fat. Bodybuilders have reportedly injected regular insulin around carbohydrate-rich meals, often alongside anabolic steroids and growth hormone, in the belief that it raises muscle glycogen, protein synthesis, size and stamina.[2][3] The look people are after is greater muscle size and fullness for a given amount of training and food, especially in the final stretch before a show, when bodybuilders also use carbohydrate loading to fill out the muscles.[3]

Reference sources describe the evidence unevenly. The Wikipedia article on insulin as a medication states that benefits are supported only in a small group of drug-naive individuals and that whether insulin improves athletic performance is unclear.[2] A 2018 review of hormones and hypertrophy covered anabolic steroids, growth hormone and IGF-1 as the agents that increase muscle mass when taken at supraphysiologic doses, especially in combination.[4] A 2024 study of recreational bodybuilders found that a large share used hormones, often with insulin or growth hormone, and that insulin use showed up in liver-enzyme and lipid markers.[4]

Insulin misuse is documented in emergency-medicine case reports of hypoglycemic coma in bodybuilders, has been mentioned as a possible factor in bodybuilder deaths, and has been prohibited for non-diabetic athletes by the International Olympic Committee since 1998.[2][4] On looksmax.org the topic appears in threads about adding insulin to testosterone and growth hormone stacks and in threads about managing insulin resistance while using growth hormone or GLP-1 compounds.[5][6][7]

paras: Insulin was the first peptide hormone discovered. It was first isolated from dog pancreas in 1921 by Frederick Banting and Charles Best in John Macleod's laboratory at the University of Toronto; Frederick Sanger sequenced it in 1951, making it the first fully sequenced protein, and Dorothy Hodgkin determined its crystal structure in 1969.[1]

Human insulin has 51 amino acids in two chains (A with 21 residues, B with 30) joined by two disulfide bonds, and the body stores it as a zinc-containing hexamer with the monomer as the active form.[1] It treats high blood glucose in type 1, type 2 and gestational diabetes and is prescription-only in Canada, the UK and the EU.[2] In the United States the FDA changed the regulatory pathway in March 2020 so that insulin products are regulated as biologics.[2]

sections.h: How it is meant to help muscle
paras: Physiologically, insulin signals muscle and fat cells to take up glucose, partly by moving GLUT4 transporters to the cell surface, and stimulates glycogen and fat synthesis, amino-acid uptake and protein synthesis while suppressing liver glucose production and fat breakdown.[1] Bodybuilders borrow this logic: an injection timed with carbohydrate-rich meals is meant to push glucose and amino acids into muscle, increasing glycogen storage and cell volume, which proponents associate with a fuller look.[2]

The Wikipedia bodybuilding article notes that carbohydrates and protein trigger insulin release, that insulin helps move glucose and amino acids into cells, and that the article describes insulin as having steroid-like effects on muscle gains; it also says bodybuilders commonly take fast-digesting sugars such as dextrose or maltodextrin around training to help replenish glycogen.[3] Advocates therefore describe injected insulin as an extension of normal post-meal physiology.

Reference sources add that exogenous insulin is said to raise glucose metabolism and peak oxygen uptake in trained athletes, while a recent assessment argues the effect applies only to a small group of drug-naive individuals and that the overall performance benefit is unclear.[2] The 2018 review of hormones and muscle hypertrophy concluded that acute hormone elevations from resistance training do not directly correspond to muscle growth, and that supraphysiologic doses of anabolic agents, especially combined, may produce large hypertrophy.[4]

According to the Wikipedia article on insulin as a medication, insulin was suggested as a performance aid around the 1998 Nagano Winter Olympics, and the International Olympic Committee banned its use by non-diabetic athletes that year; Peter Sonksen reported on it in the Journal of Endocrinology in 2001.[2] A 2008 report cited in the same article said insulin is sometimes combined with anabolic steroids and growth hormone and warned athletes of potential harm.[2]

The 2006 book Game of Shadows by San Francisco Chronicle reporters Mark Fainaru-Wada and Lance Williams alleged that baseball player Barry Bonds used insulin among other substances, reportedly because it enhances the bodybuilding effects of growth hormone; the book emerged from the BALCO investigation, and Bonds sued over its use of grand jury material before dropping the suit in June 2006.[8] The medication article also mentions insulin as a possible factor in the deaths of bodybuilders Ghent Wakefield and Rich Piana.[2]

Piana, a bodybuilder and YouTube personality who spoke openly about steroid and hormone use, collapsed at home in August 2017 and died on August 25 at age 46. His autopsy found significant heart disease and enlarged heart and liver, but no toxicology analysis was performed, so the cause and manner of death were left inconclusive.[9] His own Wikipedia article does not mention insulin, so the link comes from the medication article's wording about possible factors.[2][9]

A 2024 study in Sports Medicine - Open compared 92 male recreational bodybuilders with 45 healthy controls. About 43 percent of the bodybuilders regularly used hormones, mostly anabolic steroids, often combined with growth hormone or insulin. Insulin and growth hormone users had lower HDL cholesterol, hormone users had higher ALT and AST liver enzymes, and insulin use was specifically linked to a higher ALT-to-AST ratio. The authors suggested such markers could help anti-doping passports detect misuse.[4]

The main risk is hypoglycemia, which can progress through dizziness, weakness, confusion and seizures to coma, brain damage, paralysis or death. Other effects include low blood potassium, allergic reactions in about 2 percent of people, and firm lumps (lipohypertrophy) from repeated injections at one site.[2] Poison-centre data cited in the medication article show that most insulin exposures are unintentional.[2]

Case reports describe the bodybuilding-specific pattern. A 1998 German-language report described a 30-year-old bodybuilder who injected short-acting insulin before a competition to stimulate muscle growth, developed severe hypoglycemia with loss of consciousness and convulsions, and was stabilised with glucose and glucagon in intensive care; the authors urged repeated blood-glucose checks even in prehospital care for athletes who may be using insulin.[4] A 2019 emergency-medicine report described a 30-year-old bodybuilder in a coma from severe hypoglycemia that needed repeated glucose infusions and was later traced to covert insulin injections; the authors advised clinicians to consider exogenous insulin in patients with decreased consciousness and treatment-resistant hypoglycemia.[4]

On looksmax.org, insulin shows up in discussions about advanced 'roiding' pipelines. One thread asks why more people do not add insulin to testosterone, growth hormone and other compounds; replies there describe it as feared by many and as something few people use skillfully.[6] Another thread discusses combining growth hormone with compounds meant to reduce insulin resistance, with users debating metformin, berberine and SGLT2 inhibitors and their possible effects on mTOR and IGF-1.[5]

A further thread by a user who reports inherited insulin resistance lists fasting, chromium picolinate and other measures to improve insulin sensitivity, with replies suggesting metformin or retatrutide instead.[7] On T Nation, a participant answering a question about 'insulin manipulation' distinguished carb timing from injected insulin and said bodybuilders have injected it to improve nutrient partitioning.[10]

Because insulin is a natural hormone, detecting its injected form is harder than detecting a synthetic steroid. Rapid-acting analogs such as lispro, aspart and glulisine can be identified in urine using immunoaffinity purification and high-resolution mass spectrometry; a 2020 study in Drug Testing and Analysis reported a limit of detection of 10 pg/mL and urinary detection windows of roughly 9 hours in healthy volunteers.[4]

The Wikipedia bodybuilding article notes that the IFBB introduced doping tests and the WBF adopted a drug-testing policy in 1992, while the National Physique Committee does not require testing and the IFBB Pro League does not routinely test, so the anti-doping context differs between federations.[3]

No controlled trials have tested injected insulin as a physique aid in healthy non-diabetic bodybuilders. The medication article states that whether insulin improves athletic performance is unclear.[2] Research on bodybuilding-related use consists mainly of case reports, a cross-sectional comparison of recreational bodybuilders, and anti-doping method papers described above.[4] Large bodies of research exist on insulin in diabetes care and on exercise and insulin sensitivity in type 2 diabetes, but these concern medical treatment rather than physique goals.[11]

lore.intro: Insulin is discussed in bodybuilding and looksmaxxing forums under the nickname slin, as a nutrient-partitioning tool and as a factor to manage when using growth hormone.[5][6]
